newsitem.title: USA: Alaska governor predicts success in salmon talks.
newsitem.headline: Alaska governor predicts success in salmon talks.

text.p: The United States and Canada could have a revised version of the expired Pacific Salmon Treaty by spring if cool heads prevail when negotiations resume this fall, Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles said on Thursday.

"We would hope that there could be a conclusion, a successful agreement, probably sometime in March," Knowles said after meeting in Seattle on Wednesday with Washington Gov. Gary Locke and Canadian Fisheries Minister David Anderson.
"There's plenty of time for us to get back on track and to, I think, make it successful," the Democratic governor said in a news conference from his Juneau office.
The Wednesday meeting was part of a flurry of top-level activity that followed a three-day blockade by Canadian fishermen of an Alaska state ferry in Prince Rupert, British Columbia.

Canadian fishermen said they were angry about interception of British Columbian salmon and the failure of authorities to renew the 1985 U.S.-Canada treaty that allocates harvests of trans-boundary salmon.
Knowles, a Democrat, said "stakeholder" talks between affected commercial fishermen, excluding the area's politicians, will restart after summer's end.
Meanwhile, Anderson has been invited to an upcoming "salmon summit" to be held by Knowles, Locke, Oregon Gov. John Kitzhaber and leaders of Pacific Northwest tribes.
The governors and tribal leaders held a similar summit last year to hammer out common salmon conservation goals and management plans.
Knowles praised Anderson for trying to revive a "positive relationship." He also praised the "close teamwork" of treaty participants from Washington, Oregon and the Pacific Northwest tribes.
Not invited to the summit is British Columbia Premier Glen Clark, who supported the blockading fishermen and accused Alaska fishermen of piracy.

A top Alaska fisheries manager said stakeholders were close to agreement on Alaska-related issues when talks broke down this spring over a non-Alaska issue -- allocating salmon returning to southern British Columbia's Fraser River.

"The major point of disagreement was not over Alaska fisheries, but it was over Fraser River and Washington state fisheries," said David Benton, deputy commissioner of Alaska's Department of Fish and Game.

The dispute that sparked the ferry blockade, however, was interception of sockeye salmon bound for British Columbia's Skeena River by Alaska fishermen targeting pink salmon from Alaska's Noyes Island.
The state has sued blockade participants and the Canadian government for millions of dollars allegedly lost because of the action.
Knowles said Alaska will not resume suspended ferry service to Prince Rupert until the state is compensated for tourism losses, employee overtime and other costs.
